analysis.one_liner: Replaces much of the income tax with a 10% tax on what people buy, cutting rates on income to compensate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote in the Senate, dying in the Finance Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 10% tax on the sale of most goods and services in the United States, while cutting individual income tax rates to 15%, 25%, and 28% and cutting the corporate rate to 17%. To keep the change from hurting people with low incomes, it replaces personal exemptions with a large "family allowance" ($50,000 for a single filer, $100,000 for a married couple) and pays a rebate to low-earning workers and families with children. It would also repeal many existing credits and deductions and end the lower tax rate on capital gains. If the consumption tax collected more than 10% of the economy's output, the excess would be refunded to taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers and middle-income families would have seen most of their income taxed at lower rates or excluded entirely, and would have received wage-based rebates and child benefits to offset the new sales tax. Savers and high earners would have gained the most: taxing consumption instead of income means money that is saved or invested is never taxed, and the bill ends the special treatment of capital gains but caps all income rates at 28%. Corporations would have seen their tax rate cut from 35% to 17%.

how_it_helps.text: The family allowance would let married couples deduct up to $100,000 from taxable income before rates apply, which by itself takes most working households' income out of the income tax base.
A rebate for working taxpayers, built on earned income and child benefit amounts, would put cash back in the hands of low-wage workers and families with children.
Any consumption tax revenue above 10% of GDP would be refunded directly to individual tax filers, so the new tax could not silently grow into a revenue machine.
The corporate rate would drop to 17%, intended to make US businesses more competitive.

analysis.who_pays: Every household buying goods and services would pay the new 10% tax on purchases; the offsetting income-tax cuts and rebates only partially compensate, so people who spend nearly everything they earn would pay relatively more. Corporations that benefit from repealed deductions and credits would also lose those breaks. Businesses would bear the cost of collecting and remitting the new tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers paying a new sales tax

drawbacks.text: A 10% tax on goods and services raises prices at the register, and low- and middle-income households spend most of what they earn, so they would pay the new tax on nearly every dollar of income; the rebate offsets this only for those who qualify and only against income tax they owe.

The bill repeals many existing tax credits and deductions and ends preferential capital gains rates, so households that rely on repealed credits (education, retirement savers' credits, and others) could lose out depending on the offsetting allowance and rebate math.

Businesses would have to invoice, collect, file, and remit a new tax — an administrative burden the bill partially exempts for suppliers with $100,000 or less in annual taxable revenue, but not for most firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest trade-off: moving tax off income and onto consumption would encourage saving and could make the code simpler, but a consumption tax falls hardest on people who spend most of what they earn. Cardin's design tries to offset that with a large family allowance, wage-based rebates, and child benefits, and any revenue windfall would be refunded to households. The plan also relies on new compliance burdens for businesses of every size. But it never advanced far enough to be tested in committee or debated, so none of the distributional claims were ever scrutinized in a markup or scored through the normal process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2016, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Cardin introduced the bill on December 8, 2016, less than a month before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Finance Committee, where no further action was taken; the action history ends there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position: the current tax code stayed in place, so high-income filers and existing tax-preference industries kept the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — no tax reform happened

for.name: Sen. Ben Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, then saw it referred to the Finance Committee with no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no bipartisan coalition ever formed around it.

industries.note: The bill cuts the corporate income tax rate to 17%, a large permanent tax cut. Shareholders capture the benefit directly.
They would become collection agents for a new 10% sales-style tax, adding compliance costs, though exports are zero-rated and small suppliers under $100,000 in annual taxable revenue are exempt.

industries.industry: Tax-preparation and deduction-dependent industries (homebuilders, mortgage lenders, charities, state and local governments)
industries.note: Most itemized deductions are repealed except mortgage interest, charitable giving, state and local income taxes, and a few others, reducing the tax value of those activities.
Financial supplies are exempt from the consumption tax, but inputs used to provide them get only partial (60%) credit, a deliberate partial tax on the sector.
